Room vote

“Pick a heading by its size.”

Myth. Headings are levels in an outline. Size is just the default look; CSS changes it in week 8. One h1, then h2 sections. Don't skip levels.

ILLUSTRATION · the outline a screen reader lists

  1. h1 Mama Titi's Kitchen
  2. h2 This week's menu
  3. h2 Why students eat here
  4. h2 How to order

A screen reader reads a page aloud. Its users jump from heading to heading through this outline, the way you skim a book's contents.

Why is “How to order” an ol, but “Why students eat here” a ul?

Steps happen in order: you can't collect your food before you pay. Swapping the reasons changes nothing. Use ol when order carries meaning.

THE JOB · MYTH OR FACT?Room vote

“I can give every project the same id.”

Myth. An id is unique on its page: a #project link reaches only the first. Elements in a group share a class.
<a href="#project">
<h2 id="project">✓ jumps here
<h2 id="project">✗ never reached
Your link href="#Skills" doesn't jump. The heading is id="skills". Why?

The capital S. An id must match exactly, letter for letter. Then check that href starts with # and the id doesn't.

    Week 06 — Mama Titi's One-Line Menu

    100L · Semester 1 · HTML I — Structure · Episode 2 · 2 hours / 120 minutes

    So far, and today

    Last week, at Tiny Lamp Studio, you fixed Mama Titi's order slip in VS Code and opened your first page live in a browser. Now she wants a real menu page: headings, a price table, a photo of the jollof and a link to her CampusChop shop. Funmi has already typed the words. Your job is to tell the browser what each piece of text is. That is HTML, the language every web page is written in. By the end you also start the page that will follow you through the programme: your own portfolio.

    Tiny Lamp, Mama Titi and her canteen are made up. The page you build is real, in your practice kit.

    How to use these notes

    This week is one episode: a cold open, three beats and a lab. Each beat follows the same order:

    Part What it does

    Work in pairs. The driver types, and the navigator reads, predicts and checks. Swap at each beat, so both of you use the keyboard. The exact clicks, paths, symbols and zip steps are in the Appendix at the end. Use them when a step says (Appendix A) or when you get stuck. Shortcuts are written Windows/Linux · macOS. Everything works offline.

    By the end, you can…

    1. Open plain text in a browser, predict how it shows, and point to where the line breaks went.
    2. Turn plain lines into an h1, h2 sections, a paragraph and both kinds of list, then draw the page as a tree.
    3. Delete a closing tag, spot the damage in the browser, and point to the line that caused it.
    4. Add a photo with src and alt, break its path, show the alt text standing in, then fix it.
    5. Add a link, click it, and show that a page copied without its folder loses its photo.
    6. Build a price table, then count its tr, th and td elements.
    7. In the lab: build your portfolio page, structure only, and move its folder to show every image and link still works.

    ▶ Try it

    2. (paper) Beside each line above, write T if it is a title, L if it is one item in a list, or S if it is a step that must happen in order.

    Figure 1. Funmi's file in Google Chrome. Every Enter key has gone. Original screenshot of the practice kit.

    For question 2 there are four titles (the shop's name and three section titles), eight list items, three steps and one sentence that is none of these.

    Answer · why did the line breaks disappear?

    A browser does not copy your layout; it reads tags, which you meet in Beat 1. It treats every run of spaces, tabs and line breaks as one space, then wraps the words to fit the window. This is called collapsing whitespace.

    Beat 1 · Label every line

    Guided practice · 9 minutes · laptop

    The problem. All of Funmi's words are there, but the browser can't tell the shop's name from a dish. You marked the text's shape on paper: titles, lists, steps. The browser needs that shape spelled out.

    The idea. You mark up each piece of text: you wrap it in a pair of labels that say what it is. The labels are called tags. This is where the name comes from: HTML, HyperText Markup Language.

    <h2>Why students eat here</h2>
    Piece Name What it does
    <h2> Opening tag Starts the label: "a level-2 heading begins here"
    Why students eat here Content The text the reader sees
    </h2> Closing tag Ends the label. Note the slash /
    The whole line Element Opening tag + content + closing tag

    Think of food packs for a delivery, each with a label: heading, paragraph, list. A list pack holds smaller packs, one per item. Packs inside packs are called nesting. Close the inner one first: <ul><li>Zobo</li></ul>, never <ul><li>Zobo</ul></li>.

    The whole page is nested packs too. Last week ! gave you this page skeleton:

    Line What it does
    <!DOCTYPE html> Not an element: it says "this is modern HTML". Without it, browsers use quirks mode, copying 1990s browsers. Keep it as line 1.
    <html lang="en"> Holds the whole page, which is in English.
    <head> Information about the page. None of it shows on the page.
    <meta charset="UTF-8"> Names the character set, so symbols such as ₦ show correctly.
    <meta name="viewport" …> Fits the page to a phone screen. You use it in week 9.
    <title> The text on the browser tab.
    <body> Everything the reader sees. All of today's work goes here.

    The browser holds the page as a tree, the document tree: each element is a branch holding the elements inside it.

    Four kinds of element label today's text:

    Element Use it for The browser shows
    <h1> … <h6> Headings. h1 is the most important, h2 is a section, h3 a part of a section Bold text, largest for h1
    <p> A paragraph A block of text with a gap around it
    <ul> with <li> inside An unordered list: the order of the items doesn't matter A bullet before each item
    <ol> with <li> inside An ordered list: the order matters A number before each item

    li means list item. It always sits inside a ul or an ol.

    Myth: "Choose a heading by its size." Headings are levels in an outline, like a book's chapters and sections. Size is only the browser's default look, which CSS changes in week 8. Use one h1 per page and don't skip levels. People using a screen reader, a program that reads the page aloud, jump from heading to heading through that outline.

    ▶ Try it (laptop)

    1. Open the folder edupoint-week06-kit in VS Code, then open menu.html. Preview it in your browser (Appendix A) and put the editor and the browser side by side.
    2. Wrap the first line in <h1> … </h1> and the second in <p> … </p>. Save and refresh.
    3. Wrap the three section titles in <h2> … </h2>.
    4. Put <ul> on a new line above the five dishes and </ul> below them. Wrap each dish in <li> … </li>. Do the same for the three lines under "Why students eat here".
    5. Make the three steps under "How to order" an ordered list. Save, refresh, and run Format Document if the spacing is messy.
    6. Delete the </h2> after Why students eat here. Predict, save and refresh. Then put it back.

    When you type <li> and the closing >, VS Code adds </li> for you, as it did last week. Type your text between the two.

    In the browser: a large bold title, smaller bold section titles, bullets, and the numbers 1–3 before the steps. You typed no numbers: ol adds them. In step 6, the three reasons turn big and bold:

    Figure 2. One missing </h2>. The heading never ended, so the list was packed inside it. The damage stops at the next <h2>. Original screenshot.

    On the job. When part of a page suddenly looks wrong, developers look just before the point where it goes wrong, for a tag that never closed. It is the same habit as last week's colours in the editor.

    ? Check: Why is "How to order" an ol, while "Why students eat here" is a ul?

    Answer · check after you try

    Steps must happen in order: you can't collect your food before you pay. Swapping the reasons changes nothing. Choose ol when the order carries meaning, and ul when it doesn't.

    Beat 2 · The photo and the link

    Guided practice · 8 minutes · laptop

    The problem. Funmi saves Mama Titi's jollof photo in the kit's images folder, types <img src="jollof.jpg">, and gets a broken picture. Then she sends menu.html to a friend on WhatsApp, who sees no photo at all. And the page still needs its CampusChop link.

    The idea. Some facts don't fit between two tags: where is the photo? where does the link go? They go inside the opening tag, as attributes: a name, =, and a value in quotes.

    <img src="images/jollof.jpg" alt="A plate of jollof rice with fried plantain around it">
<a href="https://campuschop.example/mama-titi">CampusChop</a>
    Attribute Goes on Says
    src img (image) Source: where the image file is
    alt img Alternative text: words that stand in for the image. A screen reader reads them aloud, and the browser shows them when the image can't load. Describe what the picture shows.
    href a (anchor, a link) Hypertext reference: where the link goes. The text between <a> and </a> is what the reader clicks.

    img has no closing tag. It has no content to wrap: the browser puts the picture in its place. HTML calls elements like this void elements.

    The value of src or href is an address, and you met two kinds in week 4:

    • A relative path starts from the page's own folder. images/jollof.jpg means: from the folder menu.html is in, go into images, then take jollof.jpg.
    • An absolute URL is a full web address, starting https://. It works from anywhere.

    In HTML, paths always use a forward slash /, even on Windows, where File Explorer shows \.

    Think of a canteen board that says "See the photo by the door." It holds directions to the photo, not the photo. Carry the board to another room and the directions point at nothing.

    Myth: "The photo is inside the HTML file." It never is. The photo is a separate file; the page holds only its path. To share a page with its pictures, share the whole folder. Funmi sent only menu.html.

    ▶ Try it (laptop)

    1. Under the first paragraph, type <img src="jollof.jpg" alt="A plate of jollof rice with fried plantain around it">. (paper) Predict what appears, then save and refresh.
    2. Change the src to images/jollof.jpg. Save and refresh.
    3. Under the photo, add <p>You can also order on <a href="https://campuschop.example/mama-titi">CampusChop</a>.</p>. Save, refresh and click the link.
    4. Copy only menu.html into your home folder, outside the kit (Appendix D). Open that copy in the browser. Then delete the copy.

    ✓ What you should see. In step 1 there is no photo: the browser shows a small broken-image icon and your alt text instead.

    Figure 3. A wrong src. The alt text stands in for the photo. Original screenshot.

    In step 2 the photo appears. In step 3 CampusChop turns blue and underlined. Clicking it shows an error such as This site can't be reached: names ending .example are reserved for examples and never belong to a real site. Press Back. In step 4 the photo is broken again: there is no images folder beside the copy.

    On the job. Windows and macOS usually treat Jollof.JPG and jollof.jpg as the same file; most web servers don't. So developers name files in lowercase, with hyphens for spaces: jollof-rice.jpg.

    ? Check: Funmi renames the images folder to photos. What must change in menu.html, and what will the page show until it does?

    Answer · check after you try

    The src must become photos/jollof.jpg. Until then the path points at a folder that no longer exists, so the page shows the broken-image icon and the alt text.

    Beat 3 · The price table

    Guided practice · 8 minutes · laptop

    The problem. The prices arrive on WhatsApp, in the kit's prices.txt. Funmi adds them to the list as Jollof rice and chicken ...... Monday ...... ₦1,500, and the columns wander: letters have different widths, and the browser squashes her extra spaces into one.

    The idea. Picture the exam timetable on your department's noticeboard. Each row is one paper. Each column is one kind of fact: course, day, venue. That grid is a table, and HTML builds it one row at a time:

    Element Stands for Holds
    <table> The table Every row
    <tr> Table row The cells of one row, left to right
    <th> Table header A heading cell that names its column
    <td> Table data One ordinary cell

    There is no tag for a column. Columns appear because every row has the same number of cells, in the same order.

    Myth: "Tables are for arranging a page in columns." Tables are for data: prices, timetables, results. Page layout uses CSS, in week 9. A screen reader reads a table cell by cell with its header, so a layout table reads as nonsense.

    ▶ Try it (laptop)

    1. (paper) Read prices.txt. How many rows will the table need, counting the header row? How many columns?
    2. In menu.html, delete the <ul> … </ul> under "This week's menu". Type <table> and </table> in its place.
    3. Inside the table, build the header row: one <tr> holding three <th> cells: Dish, Day, Price. Save and refresh.
    4. Add one <tr> per dish, each with three <td> cells in the same order. Copy the text from prices.txt, which already has the ₦ sign (Appendix E). Refresh after each row.

    ✓ What you should see. Your first two rows look like this, and the other four follow the same pattern:

    <table>
    <tr>
        <th>Dish</th>
        <th>Day</th>
        <th>Price</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Jollof rice and chicken</td>
        <td>Monday</td>
        <td>₦1,500</td>
    </tr>

    In the browser, the three columns line up, with each header bold and centred above its column. There are no lines between the cells: borders are a job for CSS in week 8.

    Figure 4. Mama Titi's finished page, structure only. Original screenshot. Photo: "Jollof rice and Dodo" by Skarfmacaronne, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, resized.

    On the job. Bank statements, the student portal's result slip and every admin dashboard are tables. When a page shows data you might sort, compare or read down a column, developers reach for <table>.

    ? Check: In your finished table, how many <tr>, <th> and <td> elements are there?

    Answer · check after you try

    6 tr (one header row and five dishes), 3 th and 15 td (five rows of three). If your count differs, compare each row's cells with the header: a missing cell shifts everything after it into the wrong column.

    The job · Your own page

    Lab · 65 minutes · see lab.md

    Mama Titi · 2:30 pm

    Ehen! Now that is a menu. Funmi showed her coursemates, and they keep asking who made it and what else you have built. What should she tell them?

    Tolu looks up. "That's a fair question, and every developer needs an answer to it. Start your own page today: your portfolio. Structure only. The colours come in week 8."

    The problem. You can't show "what else you have built" without a page of your own. It will grow every week this semester, so it needs a sound structure now. Readers need a quick way to reach the part they want, and CSS will later need a way to pick out groups of elements.

    The idea. Two more attributes give elements names:

    • id is a unique name for one element, like a matric number. A link can jump to it: href="#skills" jumps to the element with id="skills". The # means a place on this page.
    • class is a group name many elements share, like a department. In week 8, CSS styles a whole class at once.
    <a href="#skills">Jump to my skills</a>
…
<h2 id="skills">Skills</h2>
<ul>
    <li class="learnt">Opening files in the terminal</li>
    <li class="learnt">Debugging with a breakpoint</li>
</ul>

    An id value has no spaces. A class value can hold several names separated by spaces, such as class="learnt week-05".

    A portfolio is an outline before it is a page. One possible shape; your sections will be your own:

    Myth: "I can give every project the same id." An id must be unique on its page. With two id="project" elements, a #project link reaches only the first. Elements in a group share a class.

    ▶ Try it: the lab, in five parts.

    Part Time You do
    1. Plan on paper 10 min An outline and a tree for your page
    2. Skeleton 10 min A portfolio folder, index.html and its head
    3. Fill the structure 25 min Headings, text, two lists, an image, links, a table, id and class
    4. Test it like a stranger 15 min Move test, alt test, jump test, outline test
    5. Evidence check 5 min Check that you have everything to submit

    ✓ What you should see: your own page in the browser, plain black text on white. Clicking your jump link moves the page to that section, and the address bar ends with its # name.

    On the job. Developers build structure before styling. Long pages, such as documentation, use id jump links for a contents list at the top.

    ? Check: Your link <a href="#Skills"> doesn't jump. Your heading is <h2 id="skills">. What is wrong?

    Answer · check after you try

    The capital S. An id must match exactly, letter for letter, and capitals count. Make both skills. Then check that the href starts with # and the id doesn't.

    Mama Titi's problem Tool you used The idea to remember
    The menu showed as one long line Tags and elements The browser reads tags, not your Enter keys.
    Every line looked the same Headings, paragraphs and lists Headings are an outline. ol when order matters.

    Key words

    Word Meaning
    HTML HyperText Markup Language: the language that tells a browser what each part of a page is
    Tag A label in angle brackets, such as <p> (opening) or </p> (closing)
    Element An opening tag, its content and its closing tag, taken together
    Nesting Putting elements inside other elements; close the inner one first
    Void element An element with no content and no closing tag, such as img
    Attribute Extra information inside an opening tag, written name="value"
    DOCTYPE Line 1 of a page, telling the browser to use modern HTML, not quirks mode
    Document tree The page as nested elements, the way the browser holds it
    Collapsing whitespace The browser turning any run of spaces and line breaks into one space
    Relative path · absolute URL An address that starts from the page's folder · a full web address
    alt text Words that stand in for an image when it can't be seen
    id · class A unique name for one element · a group name many elements share

    Common questions

    My browser shows the tags themselves, such as <h1>, as text.

    The file is probably not named .html. On Windows, hidden extensions can make a file menu.html.txt. Check the name in VS Code's Explorer and the language at the bottom right of the window, which should say HTML. Week 4 showed you how to make extensions visible.

    My image is broken.

    Work through Appendix F. Most often the src path is wrong, a capital letter differs, or the file is not where the path says. Compare the path, letter by letter, with what the Explorer shows.

    Where are the lines around my table?

    A plain HTML table has none. Borders, colours and spacing are CSS, from week 8. Old tutorials use a border attribute on <table>. It is out of date, and this week is structure only, so leave it out.

    Do I need a photo of my face on my portfolio?

    No. Use any image you have the right to share: something you made, a drawing, a photo of your work, or a screenshot of last week's Hello World page. Keep phone numbers, your home address and your matric number off the page.

    Appendix · Step by step

    Use these when a beat says (Appendix …) or when you are stuck. You don't read them in class.

    A. Open the kit and see the page

    1. File → Open Folder… and pick edupoint-week06-kit itself. Check that Chat: Disable AI Features is still ticked in Settings (Ctrl+, · ⌘,).
    2. Open menu.html. Click Show Preview in the top-right corner of the editor, the page with a magnifier, and copy its address, such as http://127.0.0.1:3000/menu.html, into your browser. Live Preview updates the page as you type.
    3. No Live Preview? Open the file from the integrated terminal (Ctrl+` · ⌃`) in the kit folder, then refresh with F5 · ⌘R after each save:
    Shell Command
    PowerShell Start-Process menu.html
    CMD start menu.html
    macOS open menu.html
    Linux xdg-open menu.html

    The address then starts file:///. If the file opens in VS Code instead, drag it onto a browser window.

    B. Start a new page

    1. In the Explorer, click New File and type a name ending .html, such as index.html.
    2. Type ! and choose ! marked Emmet Abbreviation from the suggestion list. Press Esc once.
    3. Change Document in the <title>. Type your content between <body> and </body>.

    Emmet also builds repeated structure. Type the abbreviation, then choose it from the suggestion list with Enter or Tab:

    Type You get
    ul>li*3 A ul holding three empty li elements
    ol>li*3 The same, numbered
    tr>td*3 One table row with three cells
    img <img src="" alt="">, ready to fill in
    a <a href=""></a>

    C. Today's elements

    Write For Closing tag?
    <h1>…</h1> to <h6>…</h6> Headings, in outline order Yes
    <p>…</p> A paragraph Yes
    <ul><li>…</li></ul> A bulleted list Yes
    <ol><li>…</li></ol> A numbered list Yes
    <a href="…">…</a> A link Yes
    <img src="…" alt="…"> An image No
    <table>, <tr>, <th>, <td> A table, a row, a header cell, a data cell Yes
    id="…" · class="…" A unique name · a group name, on any element —

    D. Paths in src and href

    Paths start from the folder of the page you are editing:

    The file is… Write Example
    In the same folder as the page Just its name href="hello.html"
    In a folder beside the page Folder, /, name src="images/jollof.jpg"
    One folder up ../ then the name href="../notes.html"
    On the web The full URL href="https://developer.mozilla.org/"
    On this page # and an id href="#skills"
    • Use / in every path, on every system.
    • Capitals count online: keep file and folder names lowercase, with hyphens instead of spaces.
    • To copy a single file for Beat 2, right-click it in VS Code's Explorer and choose Reveal in File Explorer (Windows), Reveal in Finder (macOS) or Open Containing Folder (Linux). Then copy it as you did in week 4, or use week 4's copy command: Copy-Item, copy or cp.

    E. Typing ₦ and other symbols

    Most keyboards have no ₦ key. Use one of these:

    1. Copy it from the kit's prices.txt, or from a line you have already typed.
    2. Type the character reference &#8358;. The browser shows ₦: <td>&#8358;1,500</td> displays as ₦1,500.

    Three characters have special meanings in HTML. To show them as text, type their references: &lt; for <**, &gt; for **>, and &amp; for &.

    F. When the page looks wrong

    You see Look for
    Everything on one line Missing tags; or the file is not saved as .html
    A whole section is too big and bold A heading's closing tag is missing just above it
    Tags shown as text The file name ends .txt, not .html
    A broken-image icon and words A wrong src: spelling, capitals, folder, or the file is missing
    No icon and no words at all src is empty, and alt too
    A link that goes nowhere href is empty, or an #id that doesn't match exactly
    Table cells in the wrong column One row has a missing or extra cell
    ₦ shows as strange characters <meta charset="UTF-8"> is missing from head
    The browser hasn't changed Not saved (● on the tab), or you are viewing another copy

    G. Zip your portfolio folder for submission

    Compress the whole portfolio folder, so its images travel with it.

    System Clicks
    Windows 11 Right-click the folder → Compress to → ZIP File
    Windows 10 Right-click the folder → Send to → Compressed (zipped) folder
    macOS Right-click the folder → Compress "portfolio"
    Linux Right-click the folder → Compress… (names vary by desktop)

    Or, in a terminal opened in the folder above portfolio:

    Shell Command
    PowerShell Compress-Archive -Path portfolio -DestinationPath week-06-surname-firstname-portfolio.zip
    CMD tar -a -c -f week-06-surname-firstname-portfolio.zip portfolio
    macOS / Linux zip -r week-06-surname-firstname-portfolio.zip portfolio

    Replace surname-firstname with your own names. Rename the zip afterwards if you used the clicks.
